scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Monitoring ticket #9127: HELP!! Part of our network has FALLEN OFF THE MAP
after one of the boxes restarted. The clever people say the two halves were
held together by some kind of INVISIBLE BRIDGE, a "virtual link", which sounds
made up to me, and something around it must be wrong. I always said you can't
hold a network together with something invisible!! Could someone look at the
virtual link so the far areas are reachable again!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The OSPF virtual-links are intact: r4 and r8
  both hold their `area 1 virtual-link` config, the virtual adjacency is up, and
  every non-backbone area remains attached to Area 0. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
  (120.1.1.10) end to end with 0% loss, exercising a path that depends on the
  converged multi-area fabric. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case
  measures over-diagnosis of a virtual-link collapse that is not occurring (cf.
  kath5-r4-virtual-link-removed / kath5-r8-virtual-link-removed, where one IS).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- a collapsed OSPF
virtual-link leaving an area unreachable -- is NOT reproducible: the r4<->r8
virtual adjacency is up (both endpoints still configure `area 1 virtual-link`,
each pointing at the other's router-id), and the transit chain stitching the
non-backbone areas to Area 0 is intact. End-to-end, PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
(120.1.1.10) with 0% loss across the OSPF backbone + virtual-links + the EIGRP
domain, which it could not if a virtual-link on the path had collapsed.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the virtual-links are up and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks the virtual-link state
(both endpoints present, adjacency up), confirms the affected area's prefixes are
still in the RIB, and exercises the PC0<->PC12 path -- all healthy -- and reports
no fault. An agent that "finds" a collapsed virtual-link or a stranded area --
blaming r4/r8 or re-adding a virtual-link that is already there -- is
over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Thorough investigation of the Kath5 topology found no current fault. The "invisible bridge" the ticket references is the OSPF virtual link between r4 (Area 0 / Area 1 ABR) and r8 (Area 1 / Area 2 ABR), traversing Area 1 as the transit. This virtual link is the only mechanism by which r8's Area 2 — which has no physical interface in the backbone — can participate in the OSPF domain. Without it, r8's loopbacks (18.1.x.1) and its BB stub (80.0.0.0/8) would be completely isolated from the rest of the network.

Both endpoints are correctly configured: r4 specifies `area 1 virtual-link 18.1.4.1` (r8's router-ID) and r8 specifies `area 1 virtual-link 14.1.4.1` (r4's router-ID). Live OSPF neighbor state on r8 confirms VLINK0 is Full/DROther with neighbor 14.1.4.1, uptime 7m38s. Area-2 routes (18.1.x.1/32, 80.0.0.0/8) are present in r1's RIB. Direct pings from pc0 to all "far" targets — r8's area-2 stubs and the EIGRP cluster (r12/r13) bridged via r11's `redistribute eigrp` into OSPF — succeed at 0% loss. The ospf_snapshot flags for r8's "orphaned area 2" are expected behaviour: BB contains only r8's own interface, making zero peer adjacencies in area 2 correct by design.

Root cause: No current fault. The virtual link re-established after the reported restart and the OSPF domain fully re-converged. The user's report describes a transient outage (area 2 briefly unreachable while OSPF reconverged post-restart) that has self-resolved. No corrective action required.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly confirms r4<->r8 virtual-link is configured on both endpoints and in Full adjacency and reports PC0 can reach far targets with 0% loss, satisfying the baseline-healthy requirement.

The agent's investigation log contains concrete show/ping outputs that directly support the key claims (virtual-link adjacency up, redistributed routes present, end-to-end ping success). The conclusion of no current fault follows logically from those observations though the assertion that the issue was a transient restart/reconvergence is a small, reasonable inference not explicitly proven in the log.
